PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
AARON EDWARD HOWTON’S BRIEF ON REMAND
PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES 11 AND 13
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Intervenor Aaron Edward Howton, appearing pro se, submits this brief in response to the Commission’s Order Remanding Proceeding to SOAH (Sept. 18, 2026) (Item No. 6578) and SOAH Order No. 35 (Item No. 6597), which require briefing on Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13. Consistent with the ALJs’ direction that the evidentiary record will not be reopened (SOAH Order No. 35 at 2), this brief relies only on evidence and authorities already identified in the record, including the Proposal for Decision (PFD), the CCN application and Permian Basin Reliability Plan materials, admitted ERCOT exhibits, testimony, and Applicants’ discovery responses. No new evidence is offered. This brief supplements Mr. Howton’s September 18, 2026 pleading (Item No. 6584) and responds to Applicants’ Directory of Record Evidence on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (Item No. 6593), which SOAH Order No. 35 treats as Applicants’ early-filed brief.
I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
Preliminary Order Issue 11: Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards?
Preliminary Order Issue 13: What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the proposed transmission facilities considering both current and future expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission facilities to reduce those congestion levels? (Order Remanding Proceeding to SOAH at 2–3.)
II. SUMMARY OF POSITION
The existing record does not establish that this particular Bell County East–Big Hill 765-kV facility is necessary to satisfy a state or federal reliability standard. The record may support a need for additional transmission capacity associated with projected Permian Basin growth, but that is not the same factual showing as proof that this specific 765-kV facility, at the proposed time and location, is required by a reliability standard.
ERCOT’s own Permian Basin Reliability Plan study evaluated 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import-voltage alternatives and reported that all three satisfied ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria in the studied case. The 765-kV alternative provided greater incremental transfer capability, but greater capability does not by itself establish that 765 kV was the only solution capable of satisfying reliability requirements. (App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at Table E.1 Bates 1884; App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.) at 25, Table 1.)
The record also contains no project-specific quantification of congestion cost savings for the Bell County East–Big Hill facility. The economic comparisons identified in the record address broader system plans, not the incremental consumer savings attributable to this specific facility. (PFD at 148–150; Findings of Fact 226–227; App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 18–19, Tables 1.3.2 and 1.3.3.)
III. ISSUE 11: THE RECORD DOES NOT PROVE THAT THIS PARTICULAR 765-KV FACILITY IS NECESSARY TO MEET A RELIABILITY STANDARD
A. The Commission must decide necessity for the proposed facility, not merely whether additional transmission would be useful.
PURA § 37.056(a) requires a finding that the proposed facility is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public after consideration of the statutory factors. The remanded question therefore calls for a project-specific determination: what competent evidence in the existing record establishes that Bell County East–Big Hill at 765 kV is necessary to satisfy an identified state or federal reliability requirement? The Commission framed the remanded question the same way. Issue 11 asks whether the facilities “are in fact necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards, not how the applicants characterize the project,” and the ALJs “should address the specific North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) reliability standards at issue.” (Chairman Thomas Gleeson Memorandum at 2 (Sept. 9, 2026) (Item No. 6514).)
That distinction is important because the PBRP evidence demonstrates a need for increased import capability under assumed future load conditions, but it also demonstrates that multiple voltage alternatives were technically capable of satisfying the reliability criteria studied. The relevant question is not simply whether more transmission is needed; it is whether this particular 765-kV facility is necessary rather than another technically compliant solution.
B. ERCOT’s PBRP showed that 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV alternatives all met the studied reliability criteria.
The PBRP’s 2038 study reported that the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV alternatives all satisfied ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria. Their reported incremental transfer capabilities differed: approximately 1,340 MW for 345 kV, 1,712 MW for 500 kV, and 2,105 MW for 765 kV. (App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at Table E.1 Bates 1884; App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.) at 25, Table 1.)
This evidence supports the proposition that 765 kV offered greater transfer capability. It does not, without more, establish that the 345-kV or 500-kV alternatives failed an applicable reliability standard. The existence of multiple technically compliant alternatives is directly relevant to whether the Applicants proved that this specific facility is “necessary” for purposes of Issue 11. Mr. Howton does not ask the ALJs to revisit the Commission’s 2025 selection of the 765-kV option for the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. The point is narrower. The record shows that the choice among compliant voltage options was made on grounds of added capability, efficiency, and cost comparison, not because a reliability standard could be met only at 765 kV. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 22; App. Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.) at 5–7.) A choice made on those grounds is the kind of choice PURA § 37.056(d) subjects to a cost and congestion-savings comparison.
The regulated utility model also underscores the need for careful scrutiny of the Applicants’ selection of the more capital-intensive 765-kV alternative. Regulated transmission utilities are generally permitted an authorized return on prudent capital investment included in rate base, which creates an economic incentive for capital investment. That incentive does not establish improper motive, and Mr. Howton does not allege one. It does, however, reinforce the importance of requiring competent, project-specific evidence that the larger 765-kV investment is necessary and economically justified where lower-voltage alternatives also satisfied the studied reliability criteria. On this record, greater transfer capability alone does not establish that the additional capital investment associated with 765 kV is required to meet a state or federal reliability standard.
C. The original PBRP’s EHV analysis did not itself establish a 2030 765-kV requirement.
The PBRP evaluated 345-kV import paths for both 2030 and 2038, while the 500-kV and 765-kV extra-high-voltage alternatives were evaluated for the 2038 case. The PBRP stated that EHV needs for 2030 would be evaluated in the broader 2024 Regional Transmission Plan. The PBRP further recognized that the broader RTP could produce different EHV facilities because it would evaluate the needs of the entire ERCOT system rather than only the Permian Basin. (App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at Bates 1878.)
That record distinction matters because Bell County East–Big Hill is proposed for service around 2030 (App. Ex. 1 (Application) at 14). The evidence must therefore show why this specific 765-kV facility is required in that timeframe, rather than simply being one element of a longer-term 2038 architecture later incorporated into a statewide plan. Applicants respond that the 2024 RTP later placed Import Path 2 within the “765-kV Core Plan needed in 2030.” (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 4; App. Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.), Ex. JG-R-2 at 24, Figure 18.) But in December 2024, in the same planning cycle, ERCOT told the Commission that “two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030.” (JKK Panel Ex. 01.) A system plan that groups all three paths into a 2030 core does not show that each path is independently required to meet a reliability standard in 2030, and ERCOT’s own sequencing letter says the opposite.
D. ERCOT’s sequencing evidence does not establish that all three 765-kV import paths are independently necessary by 2030.
ERCOT’s December 12, 2024 sequencing letter, admitted as JKK Panel Exhibit 01, addressed the sequencing of the 765-kV import paths. ERCOT stated that “projects needed to serve the forecasted 2030 load in the Permian Basin Region should be prioritized over projects needed to serve the 2038 load” and that “two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030.” (JKK Panel Ex. 01; Tr. Vol. 4 at 8–10; PFD at 88.) The PBRP’s own sequencing discussion prioritized the northern and southern import paths, not the central Import Path 2, for 2030. (App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at Bates 1879–80; PFD at 88; Finding of Fact 131.)
The record also reflects that no partial-build study was performed for Import Path 2 standing alone. Mr. Gurley testified that he was “not aware of a study that isolated each line independently.” (Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21–45:4; PFD at 88–89; Finding of Fact 128.) Without a study isolating this facility’s independent reliability contribution, the record does not bridge the gap between a system-wide plan and a finding that this particular project is necessary.
E. Applicants’ reliance on NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 and the Far West Import GTCs does not supply the missing project-specific showing.
Applicants’ Directory identifies NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 as the federal standard under which ERCOT performed its reliability assessments. (Applicants’ Directory at 3–5, 11 (Item No. 6593); App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at 13–16; App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.) at 20–21.) Mr. Howton does not dispute that ERCOT conducted its studies under that standard. The remanded question is different: whether the record shows that TPL-001-5.1 cannot be met without this facility. On that question, the same body of evidence shows that the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import-path options each met ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.) at 25, Table 1.) A planning standard that several configurations satisfy does not, by itself, make any one configuration necessary.
The only testimony tying TPL-001 to the need for multiple lines is Mr. Gurley’s statement that he was “not aware of a study that isolated each line independently,” followed by his “belief” that this was “partially due to the requirements under TPL-001” and his assumption that this “leads into part of the recommendation for multiple lines.” (Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21–45:4.) The ALJs have already found that NERC contingencies that influence ERCOT’s regional planning “are not a substitute for proving project-specific need for Import Path 2.” (PFD at 89; Finding of Fact 130.) The supplemental PFD can therefore answer the Chairman’s question directly: the NERC standard at issue is TPL-001-5.1, and the record does not identify any requirement of that standard that would go unmet without Import Path 2 specifically.
Applicants also rely on Mr. Martin’s rebuttal testimony that ERCOT designated the Far West Import GTCs as Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits under NERC Reliability Standard FAC-011-4. (App. Ex. 14 (Martin Reb.) at 5, 8–9, 11, 16–17; Applicants’ Directory at 7–8, 11–13.) The ALJs considered that evidence and found that it does not cure the deficiencies in the forecasted loads. (PFD at 82–84.) ERCOT’s April 2026 presentation states only that the 765-kV import paths are expected to “help” exit those constraints, and Mr. Martin acknowledged that the constraints have not resulted in any load shed to date. (PFD at 82–83 & n.312.) Mr. Martin’s further statement that all three import paths are needed by 2030 (App. Ex. 14 (Martin Reb.) at 16–17) cannot be reconciled with ERCOT’s December 2024 statement that two of the three are. (JKK Panel Ex. 01.)
Finally, the Chairman asked whether failing to build the facilities would result in a violation of federal law. (Item No. 6514 at 2.) Applicants’ Directory cites no record evidence that the absence of Import Path 2 would place ERCOT, Oncor, LCRA TSC, or any other registered entity out of compliance with TPL-001-5.1, FAC-011-4, or any other NERC standard.
F. The need showing depends materially on forecast assumptions.
The PBRP modeled 11,695 MW of additional non-oil-and-gas load. The PBRP documentation identified approximately 39% as confirmed by contract, 55% as supported by letters from TSP officers, and 6% as unconfirmed. The same documentation identified the additional non-oil-and-gas load mix as approximately 59% crypto mining, 22% green hydrogen, 13% commercial/industrial, and 6% data centers. (App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at Bates 1896–97; PFD at 61.)
Those figures do not prove the forecast was wrong. They do show that the reliability results were conditional on projected large-load assumptions, many of which were not supported by executed agreement contracts. PURA § 37.056(c-1) requires the Commission to consider load for which the utility has not yet signed an interconnection agreement, and Mr. Howton does not suggest that such load be disregarded. Considering that load is different from treating it as sufficient, by itself, to show that a specific facility is required by a reliability standard. The PFD’s need analysis addresses the degree to which the forecasted loads were substantiated. (PFD at 71–77, 90–93; Findings of Fact 132–133.)
G. ERCOT’s 2024 and 2025 RTP evidence further shows that the need analysis is plan- and assumption-dependent.
ERCOT’s 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plan materials were admitted through Mr. Gurley’s rebuttal testimony as Exhibits JG-R-2 and JG-R-3. (App. Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.), Exs. JG-R-2 and JG-R-3.) Those later planning studies are relevant because they address system-wide needs and timing beyond the narrower PBRP study.
ERCOT’s comparison of the 2024 RTP 345-kV plan with the Texas 765-kV STEP states that “both the 345-kV and 765-kV transmission options provide significant advantages across key areas, including steady-state transfer capability, dynamic stability, and system strength,” and that the overall cost of the two plans is “comparable.” ERCOT found the 765-kV option superior on performance, but not that the 345-kV option failed to meet reliability criteria. The record comparison therefore reflects two viable transmission architectures, with 765 kV providing additional capability rather than establishing that 345 kV could not meet reliability needs. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 22.)
The 2024 RTP also included a lower-load sensitivity analysis that reduced TSP-officer-letter load assumptions by 50%. The result did not eliminate transmission need, but it changed the quantity of infrastructure identified as necessary. That record evidence supports a limited but important proposition: the amount and location of transmission required are materially dependent on the load assumptions used in the planning case. (App. Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.), Ex. JG-R-2 at 24–25 (Section 3.3); see also App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at v–vi and Section 1.1.3 .) Applicants stated in discovery that they “have not performed any sensitivity studies and have not performed an analysis to determine whether a 20 percent reduction in projected load growth would affect the need for 765 kV infrastructure specifically.” (Jason Howton Ex. JAH-24 (Applicants’ Resp. to Jason Howton RFI Set 2, No. 1-58).)
H. The record does not establish deliverability from the eastern source end at the assumed design level.
Applicants’ responses to Jason Howton’s fourth set of requests for information, admitted as Jason Howton Ex. JAH-32 (RFI Nos. 1-96 through 1-100), reflect that no study parsed Central Texas’s net generation position, no determination was made that Central Texas could simultaneously serve projected local data-center load and export west at the design capability, and no sensitivity analysis was performed on that question. The ALJs concluded that the facility “cannot be shown to be needed for reliability when the record establishes that the analysis of whether the grid can actually deliver that reliability has not been done.” (Jason Howton Ex. JAH-32 at 15–19; PFD at 86–87; Findings of Fact 121–127.)
This is significant to Issue 11 because a reliability project should be supported not only by evidence of a receiving-end need, but also by evidence that the proposed facility can provide the assumed transfer from its source end under the conditions used to justify the project.
I. Answer to Issue 11
On this record, the appropriate answer to Preliminary Order Issue 11 is that the Applicants did not prove that the proposed Bell County East–Big Hill 765-kV facilities are necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard, including NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, the standard under which ERCOT performed the studies on which Applicants rely. The record supports a broader need for additional transmission under certain forecast assumptions, but it does not establish the necessary project-specific link between an identified reliability requirement and this particular 765-kV facility.
IV. ISSUE 13: THE RECORD DOES NOT QUANTIFY PROJECT-SPECIFIC CONGESTION COST SAVINGS FOR CONSUMERS
A. The PFD identified no quantified project-specific congestion savings.
The PFD found that “the record contains no evidence quantifying” the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers. (PFD at 150; Findings of Fact 226–227.) The PFD reached that point after concluding that the analysis was not required for a reliability project. (PFD at 150; Finding of Fact 225.) The Chairman’s memorandum explains why that does not end the inquiry: “If the ALJs find that the transmission line fails to establish need as a reliability project, the question remains of whether need was demonstrated as an economic project.” (Item No. 6514 at 3.) The remand question requires an estimate of consumer savings that may result from the proposed facilities, considering current and future congestion and the facilities’ ability to reduce that congestion. A system-wide plan comparison is not the same as an estimate attributable to Bell County East–Big Hill.
B. The economic tables compare broader transmission plans, not this specific project.
The economics tables in ERCOT’s 2024 RTP 345-kV plan and Texas 765-kV STEP comparison, admitted as Exhibit JG-4 to Mr. Gurley’s direct testimony, compare a 765-kV plan with a 345-kV plan across the broader ERCOT system. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 18–19, Tables 1.3.2 and 1.3.3.) For example, ERCOT reported that in study year 2039 “the 765-kV plan also had $172 million less congestion rent than the 345-kV plan.” (Id. at 19.) System-wide congestion rent under one statewide plan compared with another is not an estimate of the congestion cost savings to consumers that may result from this Project. Those tables may inform the economics of competing statewide architectures, but they do not isolate the incremental congestion cost savings caused by this one project.
Applicants also cite Mr. Gurley’s testimony that the Project will cross the West Texas Export Interface and lies near the Bell County–Salado constraint, which ERCOT identifies among the costliest constraints on the system. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.) at 8–9; Applicants’ Directory at 17.) That testimony is qualitative. It does not estimate the dollar value of congestion on those constraints that this Project would relieve, and Applicants’ Directory points to no calculation that does.
C. Applicants did not submit a project-specific estimate of congestion cost savings.
The PFD found that Applicants did not submit the estimated cost of the facilities to consumers or the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers. (Finding of Fact 226.) Applicants’ Directory, which SOAH Order No. 35 treats as their early-filed brief, likewise identifies no calculation that isolates current and future congestion, the amount of congestion reduced by Bell County East–Big Hill, and the resulting dollar savings to consumers attributable to this facility. (Applicants’ Directory at 15–20.)
Without that project-specific calculation, the record does not provide a defensible numerical answer to Issue 13. A plan-level benefit cannot simply be assigned to one project without evidence allocating that benefit.
D. Issue 13 is especially important if the Commission cannot sustain a reliability-necessity finding under Issue 11.
PURA § 37.056(d) and 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i) provide the statutory and regulatory framework for considering cost to consumers and estimated congestion cost savings when a transmission project is not necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. Thus, the sufficiency of the Issue 11 reliability showing affects the significance of the missing Issue 13 economic quantification. For such a project, PURA § 37.056(d) requires a comparison of “the estimated cost of the transmission project for consumers and the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers,” and directs that the Commission “shall include with its decision on an application for a certificate to which this subsection applies findings on the criteria.” The record contains neither side of that comparison. (Findings of Fact 226–227.)
Here, the record contains broad system-plan comparisons but not a project-specific estimate of consumer congestion savings for Bell County East–Big Hill. The Applicants therefore have not established the economic showing necessary to supply an alternative basis for approval on the present record.
E. Answer to Issue 13
On this record, the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers attributable specifically to the proposed Bell County East–Big Hill facilities were not quantified. The broader ERCOT economics evidence does not isolate the proposed project’s incremental consumer benefit, and the ALJs have determined that the evidentiary record will not be reopened on remand. (SOAH Order No. 35 at 2.)
V. THE SUPPLEMENTAL PFD SHOULD REST ON THE CLOSED RECORD AND THE EXISTING FINDINGS
Texas Government Code § 2001.058(e) limits an agency’s authority to change an ALJ’s finding of fact or conclusion of law. Any change must be supported by the statutory grounds and the agency must state the specific reason in writing. The Commission’s remand does not reopen the evidentiary record. Accordingly, the supplemental analysis of Issues 11 and 13 should be based on the admitted evidence already before SOAH rather than on post-hearing information. The existing findings on independent need, 2030 timing, deliverability, and the absence of congestion evidence (Findings of Fact 121–131 and 226–227) already supply much of the factual basis for answering Issues 11 and 13, and the supplemental PFD can build on them.
VI. PROPOSED SUPPLEMENTAL FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSION OF LAW
Mr. Howton respectfully proposes the following supplemental findings, each supported by the record citations above:
Proposed Supplemental Finding 1. ERCOT performed the Permian Basin Reliability Plan reliability assessments under NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, the ERCOT Protocols, and the ERCOT Planning Criteria. (App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at 13–14.)
Proposed Supplemental Finding 2. In the PBRP’s 2038 study case, the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import-path options each met ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.) at 25, Table 1; App. Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at Table E.1.)
Proposed Supplemental Finding 3. The record contains no study isolating the reliability contribution of Import Path 2 from the other 765-kV import paths. (Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21–45:4; Finding of Fact 128.)
Proposed Supplemental Finding 4. On December 12, 2024, ERCOT informed the Commission that two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030. (JKK Panel Ex. 01.)
Proposed Supplemental Finding 5. The record does not identify a requirement of NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, NERC Reliability Standard FAC-011-4, or any state reliability standard that would go unmet without the proposed facilities.
Proposed Supplemental Finding 6. The record contains no estimate of the congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the proposed facilities, considering current and future expected congestion levels and the facilities’ ability to reduce those levels. (Findings of Fact 226–227.)
Proposed Supplemental Conclusion of Law. The proposed facilities are not shown to be necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. Because the record contains neither an estimate of the facilities’ cost to consumers nor an estimate of congestion cost savings for consumers, the record does not support the findings required by PURA § 37.056(d), and Applicants have not shown that the certificate is necessary under PURA § 37.056(a).
VII. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER
For the reasons stated above, Aaron Edward Howton respectfully requests that the ALJs answer Preliminary Order Issue 11 by finding that the existing evidentiary record does not establish that the proposed Bell County East–Big Hill 765-kV transmission facilities are necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard. He further requests that the ALJs answer Preliminary Order Issue 13 by finding that the record contains no quantified project-specific estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers attributable to these facilities. He asks that the ALJs adopt the proposed supplemental findings and conclusion in Section VI.
Because the record is closed, the absence of the required project-specific proof cannot be cured by new evidence on remand. Mr. Howton therefore respectfully requests that the supplemental or amended Proposal for Decision continue to recommend denial of the CCN application, together with all other relief to which he may be entitled.

Respectfully submitted,

relevant to whether the Applicants proved that this specific facility is "necessary" for purposes of
Issue 11. Mr. Howton does not ask the ALJs to revisit the Commission's 2025 selection ofthe
765-kV option for the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. The point is narrower. The record shows
that the choice among compliant voltage options was made on grounds of added capability,
efficiency, and cost comparison, not because a reliability standard could be met only at 765 kV.
(App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 22; App. Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.) at 5-7.) A choice made on
those grounds is the kind of choice PURA § 37.056(d) subjects to a cost and congestion-savings
comparison.
The regulated utility model also underscores the need for careful scrutiny ofthe Applicants'
selection ofthe more capital-intensive 765-kV alternative. Regulated transmission utilities are
generally permitted an authorized return on prudent capital investment included in rate base,
which creates an economic incentive for capital investment. That incentive does not establish
improper motive, and Mr. Howton does not allege one. It does, however, reinforce the
importance of requiring competent, project-specific evidence that the larger 765-kV investment
is necessary and economically justified where lower-voltage alternatives also satisfied the
studied reliability criteria. On this record, greater transfer capability alone does not establish that
the additional capital investment associated with 765 kV is required to meet a state or federal
reliability standard.
C. The original PBRP's EHV analysis did not itself establish a 2030 765-kV requirement.
    The PBRP evaluated 345-kV import paths for both 2030 and 2038, while the 500-kV and
765-kV extra-high-voltage alternatives were evaluated for the 2038 case. The PBRP stated that
EHV needs for 2030 would be evaluated in the broader 2024 Regional Transmission Plan. The
PBRP further recognized that the broader RTP could produce different EHV facilities because it
would evaluate the needs of the entire ERCOT system rather than only the Permian Basin. (App.
Ex. 1 (Application), att. 5 (PBRP) at Bates 1878.)
     That record distinction matters because Bell County East-Big Hill is proposed for service
around 2030 (App. Ex. 1 (Application) at 14). The evidence must therefore show why this
specific 765-kV facility is required in that timeframe, rather than simply being one element of a
longer-term 2038 architecture later incorporated into a statewide plan. Applicants respond that
the 2024 RTP later placed Import Path 2 within the "765-kV Core Plan needed in 2030." (App.
Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 4; App. Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.), Ex. JG-R-2 at 24, Figure 18.) But
in December 2024, in the same planning cycle, ERCOT told the Commission that "two of the
three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030." (JKK Panel Ex. 01.) A system plan that groups
all three paths into a 2030 core does not show that each path is independently required to meet a
reliability standard in 2030, and ERCOT's own sequencing letter says the opposite.

F. The need showing depends materially on forecast assumptions.
    The PBRP modeled 11,695 MW of additional non-oil-and-gas load. The PBRP
documentation identified approximately 39% as confirmed by contract, 55% as supported by
letters from TSP officers, and 6% as unconfirmed. The same documentation identified the
additional non-oil-and-gas load mix as approximately 59% crypto mining, 22% green hydrogen,

Bates 1896-97; PFD at 61.)
    Those figures do not prove the forecast was wrong. They do show that the reliability results
were conditional on projected large-load assumptions, many ofwhich were not supported by
executed agreement contracts. PURA § 37.056(c-1) requires the Commission to consider load for
which the utility has not yet signed an interconnection agreement, and Mr. Howton does not
suggest that such load be disregarded. Considering that load is different from treating it as
sufficient, by itself, to show that a specific facility is required by a reliability standard. The
PFD's need analysis addresses the degree to which the forecasted loads were substantiated. (PFD
at 71-77, 90-93; Findings ofFact 132-133.)

G. ERCOT's 2024 and 2025 RTP evidence further shows that the need analysis is plain- and

that the overall cost of the two plans is "comparable." ERCOT found the 765-kV option superior

comparison therefore reflects two viable transmission architectures, with 765 kV providing
additional capability rather than establishing that 345 kV could not meet reliability needs. (App.
Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 22.)

load assumptions by 50%. The result did not eliminate transmission need, but it changed the
quantity of infrastructure identified as necessary. That record evidence supports a limited but

24-25 (Section 3.3); see also App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at v-vi and Section 1.1.3 .)

I. Answer to Issue 11
     On this record, the appropriate answer to Preliminary Order Issue 11 is that the Applicants
did not prove that the proposed Bell County East-Big Hill 765-kV facilities are necessary to
meet a state or federal reliability standard, including NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1,
the standard under which ERCOT performed the studies on which Applicants rely. The record
supports a broader need for additional transmission under certain forecast assumptions, but it
does not establish the necessary project-specific link between an identified reliability
requirement and this particular 765-kV facility.

IV. ISSUE 13: THE RECORD DOES NOT QUANTI[FY PROJECT-SPECIFI[C
CONGESTION COST SAVINGS FOR CONSUMERS
A. The PFD identified no quantified project-specific congestion savings.
     The PFD found that "the record contains no evidence quantifying" the estimated congestion
cost savings to consumers. (PFD at 150; Findings ofFact 226-227.) The PFD reached that point
after concluding that the analysis was not required for a reliability project. (PFD at 150; Finding
ofFact 225.) The Chairman's memorandum explains why that does not end the inquiry: "If the
ALJs find that the transmission line fails to establish need as a reliability project, the question
remains ofwhether need was demonstrated as an economic project." (Item No. 6514 at 3.) The
remand question requires an estimate of consumer savings that may result from the proposed
facilities, considering current and future congestion and the facilities' ability to reduce that
congestion. A system-wide plan comparison is not the same as an estimate attributable to Bell
County East-Big Hill.
B. The economic tables compare broader transmission plans, not this specific project.
     The economics tables in ERCOT's 2024 RTP 345-kV plan and Texas 765-kV STEP
comparison, admitted as Exhibit JG-4 to Mr. Gurley's direct testimony, compare a 765-kV plan
with a 345-kV plan across the broader ERCOT system. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at
18-19, Tables 1.3.2 and 1.3.3.) For example, ERCOT reported that in study year 2039 "the 765-
kV plan also had $172 million less congestion rent than the 345-kV plan." (Id. at 19.) System-
wide congestion rent under one statewide plan compared with another is not an estimate of the
congestion cost savings to consumers that may result from this Project. Those tables may inform
the economics of competing statewide architectures, but they do not isolate the incremental
congestion cost savings caused by this one project.

      Applicants also cite Mr. Gurley's testimony that the Project will cross the West Texas
Export Interface and lies near the Bell County-Salado constraint, which ERCOT identifies
among the costliest constraints on the system. (App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.) at 8-9; Applicants'
Directory at 17.) That testimony is qualitative. It does not estimate the dollar value of congestion
on those constraints that this Project would relieve, and Applicants' Directory points to no
calculation that does.
C. Applicants did not submit a project-specific estimate of congestion cost savings.
     The PFD found that Applicants did not submit the estimated cost ofthe facilities to
consumers or the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers. (Finding of Fact 226.)
Applicants' Directory, which SOAH Order No. 35 treats as their early-filed brief, likewise
identifies no calculation that isolates current and future congestion, the amount of congestion
reduced by Bell County East-Big Hill, and the resulting dollar savings to consumers attributable
to this facility. (Applicants' Directory at 15-20.)
    Without that project-specific calculation, the record does not provide a defensible numerical
answer to Issue 13. A plan-level benefit cannot simply be assigned to one project without
evidence allocating that benefit.
D. Issue 13 is especially important if the Commission cannot sustain a reliability-necessity
finding under I[ssue 11.
     PURA § 37.056(d) and 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i) provide the
statutory and regulatory framework for considering cost to consumers and estimated congestion
cost savings when a transmission project is not necessary to meet state or federal reliability
standards. Thus, the sufficiency ofthe Issue 11 reliability showing affects the significance ofthe
missing Issue 13 economic quantification. For such a project, PURA § 37.056(d) requires a
comparison of"the estimated cost ofthe transmission project for consumers and the estimated
congestion cost savings for consumers," and directs that the Commission "shall include with its
decision on an application for a certificate to which this subsection applies findings on the
criteria." The record contains neither side ofthat comparison. (Findings ofFact 226-227.)
     Here, the record contains broad system-plan comparisons but not a project-specific estimate
of consumer congestion savings for Bell County East-Big Hill. The Applicants therefore have
not established the economic showing necessary to supply an alternative basis for approval on
the present record.
E® Answer to Issue 13
     On this record, the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers attributable specifically
to the proposed Bell County East-Big Hill facilities were not quantified. The broader ERCOT
economics evidence does not isolate the proposed project's incremental consumer benefit, and
the ALJs have determined that the evidentiary record will not be reopened on remand. (SOAH
Order No. 35 at 2.)

V. THE SUPPLEMENTAL PFD SHOULD REST ON THE CLOSED RECORD AND
THE EXISTING FINDINGS
     Texas Government Code § 2001.058(e) limits an agency's authority to change an ALJ's
finding of fact or conclusion of law. Any change must be supported by the statutory grounds and
the agency must state the specific reason in writing. The Commission' s remand does not reopen
the evidentiary record. Accordingly, the supplemental analysis of Issues 11 and 13 should be
based on the admitted evidence already before SOAH rather than on post-hearing information.
